explanations.explanation: Mercy it is. David says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). He doesn't come in with a list of his good points. He just says he's frail and asks for mercy, and I think that's about the most honest way to walk into any prayer.

Wisdom is a good thing to ask for, but it isn't what David asks for here. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). Right now he isn't looking for answers. He's looking for mercy, and it's the next thing out of his mouth.

Victory sounds like a very kingly thing to ask for, friend. But David doesn't ask for it here. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail…" (Psalm 6:2). He asks for mercy, because he knows he's frail.

Nope, it's the opposite. David doesn't say he's strong at all. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony." (Psalm 6:2). A man who says he's frail and asks to be healed isn't pretending to do this on his own.

That's right. David never claims to be strong enough. He says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony." (Psalm 6:2). He asks the LORD for mercy and healing, and I think there's real strength in saying that out loud.

Yes, ma'am, yes, sir, it goes deeper than the bones. David says, "My soul is deeply distressed." (Psalm 6:3). First his bones hurt, and now his soul hurts too. I think this is a heavy part of the psalm, so let it sit for a second.

David actually says it goes further than that. Right after the bones, he says, "My soul is deeply distressed." (Psalm 6:3). So the hurt is in his body and in his soul, and he brings both of them to the LORD.
That's the one. David says, "Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). He doesn't point to anything he's done. He points to who the LORD is.

The LORD is powerful, no question, but that's not the reason David gives here. He says, "Save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). He leans on the LORD's loving devotion, not on His strength.

Good guess, but David doesn't bring up the LORD's reputation in this verse. He says, "Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your loving devotion." (Psalm 6:4). His reason is the LORD's loving devotion, plain and simple.

Not quite. David says the opposite: "For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?" (Psalm 6:5). Sheol is the place of the dead. He asks it as a question, and the question tells you he doesn't expect praise from there.

Right. David says, "For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?" (Psalm 6:5). Sheol is the place of the dead. He's saying no one mentions the LORD in death, and I think he's telling the LORD he wants to keep praising Him while he's alive.
All night, friend. David says, "all night I flood my bed with weeping" (Psalm 6:6). He isn't crying for a minute and moving on. This is a whole night of it.
Actually, the weeping goes on all night. David says, "all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears." (Psalm 6:6). So this isn't a quick cry. It lasts through the whole night.
That's it. David says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). All that weeping through the night wears him out, eyes and all.
I wish, but this is the low point of the psalm. David says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). Hope shows up a few verses later, but it hasn't arrived yet.
It goes the other way, friend. David says, "My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes." (Psalm 6:7). Grief has his eyes growing dim, not sharper.

explanations.answer: The LORD has heard his weeping
explanations.explanation: Yes! David says, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). Nothing about his troubles has been fixed in that verse. What changed is that he knows the LORD has heard him.

explanations.answer: His tears have finally dried up
explanations.explanation: Not this time. David gives a different reason: "for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). He doesn't say the tears stopped. He says the LORD heard them.

explanations.answer: His army has just shown up
explanations.explanation: A king with an army would make a nice story, but that's not what's in the verse. David says, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping." (Psalm 6:8). His confidence comes from the LORD hearing him, not from any soldiers.
Accepted! David says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." (Psalm 6:9). He says it about the same prayer he started with, the one in all the tears.
No, David says the very opposite. He says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." (Psalm 6:9). He sounds sure that his prayer was not turned away.

I get why you'd think that, since David asked "How long?" back in verse 3 (Psalm 6:3). But by verse 9 he says, "The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer." (Psalm 6:9). He says accepts, not delayed.

explanations.answer: They will turn back in disgrace
explanations.explanation: That's right. David says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). Notice the word sudden. It won't be a slow fade.

explanations.answer: They will win in the end
explanations.explanation: That's not where David lands. He says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). The one who ends up turning back is the enemy, not David.

That would be a sweet ending, but the verse doesn't say it. David says, "All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace." (Psalm 6:10). Ashamed and dismayed is how he sees it going.
